Theon International (THEON-NL): investment memo

Theon is a predictable 26%-margin compounder priced for its balance-sheet worry; its re-rating waits on a dated leverage test or a sale of its 283 EURm Exosens stake

As at 3 November 2026. Share price 30.42 EUR (close on 30 October 2026); market value about 2.4 EURbn on 78.6m diluted shares. Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model after update 2; consensus is the FactSet median at 28 October 2026. Bases, sources and a glossary of acronyms are in the end notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one sentence. Theon's operating lines are among the most predictable in European defence (contracted demand, supply-paced growth and a flat 26% margin), but they are bolted to a balance sheet that faces a dated leverage test whose outcome is close to a coin toss, and management holds a liquid 283 EURm stake in its supplier Exosens that can settle that test on any day it chooses.

2.4xsoft backlog plus options over the FY2026 revenue guide
26.4%adjusted EBIT margin, flat to FY2030
2.9xpeak leverage, mid-2027; tested at dated prints
283 EURmliquid, tax-free Exosens stake; 30% chance of a sale in 18 months
76%of daily variance is Theon's own; P/E 15.1x vs peers 20x to 28x

The ten things that matter.

  1. 1
    Demand is not the debate. Theon's soft backlog of 1.46 EURbn plus 902 EURm of contractual options equals 2.4x the FY2026 revenue guidance of about 600 EURm, and about 500 EURm of FY2027 revenue is already scheduled. NATO's 3.5% spending floor, Germany's 180 EURbn and the EU's 150 EURbn Security Action for Europe (SAFE) loans run to 2030 to 2035. Even the bear case has FY2027 revenue growing 14%.
  2. 2
    The ceiling on growth is tube supply, not orders. Exosens has contracted "well over 400,000" image-intensifier tubes to Theon for 2026 to 2030 (about 80,000 to 90,000 a year), and Harder Digital adds about 13,000 a year for internal use. The 1 EURbn programme of the Organisation for Joint Armament Co-operation (OCCAR) alone needs about 67,000 tubes a year in 2027 to 2029. Night-vision revenue therefore grows about 11% in FY2027 and 4% to 7% a year after, so group growth from FY2028 depends on the third of revenue outside night vision. FY2028 and FY2029 consensus revenue (870 and 988 EURm) does not carry the tube cap; the model is 2% and 4% below. The tube cap is the largest disagreement with consensus, and most brokers have not yet written it into their numbers.
  3. 3
    The margin is a flat line, not a lever. The adjusted EBIT margin holds at 26.2% to 26.5% through FY2030 because two sets of forces cancel: OCCAR's competitive pricing and wage localisation pull the margin down, while HGH's EBITDA margin above 40% and tube-free thermal and digital products pull it up. Operating leverage is low (a 10% revenue move is an 11% to 13% EBIT move) and asymmetric (tube supply caps the upside; nothing caps the downside). EBIT growth therefore equals revenue growth: better than the eight points of margin lost over FY2021 to FY2025, but worse than management's "mix shift to software" narrative implies.
  4. 4
    The lines below EBIT pay for the strategy before they benefit from it. Net financial items go from -6.8 EURm in FY2025 to -27 EURm in FY2027; the tax rate steps up to 25% (the H1 2026 underlying rate was near 30%); the Exosens stake pays no dividend; and minority interests rise. Adjusted EPS therefore grows 18% in FY2026 against adjusted EBIT growth of 38% (the rights issue enlarged the share count), roughly matches EBIT growth in FY2027 (+23% against +25%), and outgrows EBIT from FY2028 as deleveraging adds 1 to 2 points a year.
  5. 5
    Cash is the weak line, and it improves mechanically. Free cash flow was 17% of net income in FY2025 and rises to 32, 63, 94 and 120 EURm over FY2026 to FY2029 (conversion rising from 26% to 68%). The improvement comes from slower growth (working-capital absorption falls from 48 to 27 EURm a year), not from a much lower working-capital ratio (42.5% falling to 39% of revenue). Consensus free cash flow is 19% to 26% too high through FY2028, which makes free cash flow the line most likely to disappoint and the one the sell-side revises least.
  6. 6
    Leverage is the hinge, and its test is dated. Net debt peaks at about 575 EURm (2.9x EBITDA) in mid-2027 after the 290 EURm HGH payment, and ends 2027 at about 2.48x against the company's target of "below 2.5x in 2027". One point of working capital (7.5 EURm) or 15 EURm of EBITDA would tip the year-end ratio above 2.5x. The covenant is 3.5x (a 16% EBITDA cushion) unless the 300 EURm revolving facility still carries the 3.0x of the December 2025 information memorandum (a 2% cushion); the company has not said which level applies. The dated prints are 19 March 2027 (end-2026 net debt, about 250 EURm in the model), September 2027 (June 2027 leverage) and March 2028 (end-2027 leverage).
  7. 7
    The Exosens stake is the asymmetry. Theon owns 4.98m Exosens shares, worth about 283 EURm at 56.9 EUR. The stake is liquid, tax-free to sell under Cyprus law and pays no dividend; the tube supply agreement to 2030 is legally independent of it; and in September 2026 management abandoned the board-seat rationale for holding it. A sale would take end-2027 leverage to about 1.1x, add about 5% to FY2028 EPS, end the covenant question and remove ±0.36 EUR of reported-EPS noise per 10% move in Exosens' share price. I put the probability of a sale inside 18 months at 30%, higher if the covenant tightens. End-2027 leverage is therefore bimodal (about 1.1x with a sale, 2.3x to 2.8x without), not a bell curve.
  8. 8
    The market has priced the worry, not the resolution. Theon trades at a 24-month-forward P/E of 15.1x (the 42nd percentile of five years and the 24th of two years) against electronics peers at 20x to 28x. The shares fell 12.6% over three months while MilDef rose 12.6% and Hensoldt 7.9%, and 76% of Theon's daily share-price variance is stock-specific. Over twelve months, FY2027 EBITDA estimates rose 16% while FY2027 EPS estimates fell 3%. Rising estimates, a falling multiple and a dated catalyst form the pattern of a bottoming stock, and all seven brokers still rate the shares Buy with targets near 40 EUR.
  9. 9
    The return is earnings-led, with a de-rating drag. At the 14.8x guideline multiple, the model gives a total return of +12.8% to 31 December 2027 (earnings +22.2%, multiple -9.6%, dividends +2.4%) and +29.2% to 30 June 2029 (earnings +38.6%, multiple -9.6%, dividends +3.9%). The multiple is the swing factor: at the two-year median of 17x the 18-month return is about +29%, and at the 11.8x trough band it is about -10%.
  10. 10
    Five judgements move the shares, and leverage links them (the arithmetic is in topic #9). The five are: a one-quarter slip in OCCAR or German call-offs (EPS -6%, leverage +0.2x, the 2.5x target missed); the working-capital ratio (three points equal 22 EURm and decide the 2.5x target, but move EPS by only 0.01 EUR); a stake sale (EPS +5%, leverage -1.3x); the tube cap on FY2028 revenue (consensus 2% to 7% too high); and one point of margin (EPS ±4.4%). A ceasefire or a Bundestag delay would hit the first two judgements and the stake's value in the same half-year as the leverage peak.

The practical implication: hold through 10 to 11 months of good news that will not move the shares. The market has stopped paying for the predictable half of the case (revenue, EBIT and guidance raises) and is pricing the unpredictable half (cash and leverage). The operating prints between now and March 2027 will almost certainly be good and will almost certainly not re-rate the stock. The re-rating event is either the dated leverage print in September 2027 or a management decision to sell the Exosens stake, which could come on any day. The skew of fundamental outcomes is modestly positive; the skew of upgrade probability is positive on EBIT and negative on EPS until the balance-sheet question closes.

Scorecard: the grades for topics 1 to 12

The Rater's scores. A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24.

#1Tailwinds in the operating environmentB83#2Internal change forcesC66#3Industry, business model and managementC66#4Guidance, sell-side and delivery recordB76#5Pricing power and operating leverageD30#6Forecast financialsA91#7Scope for upgrades in 6 to 12 monthsD45#8Current momentumC54#9Riskiness and simplicityD42#10Lifecycle phaseC57#11The fair multipleC62#12Total shareholder returnC53

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Conclusion: demand is structural, contracted and floored by policy to 2029, so Theon's tailwind is as strong as any in European equities. The headwinds are real, but they act on supply timing, financing cost and the multiple rather than on whether the revenue exists.

Four accelerating external drivers meet at Theon's product.

  • Budgets: European rearmament budgets are floored by policy to 2035.
  • Soldier modernisation: armies are equipping soldiers on a 1:1 basis; European night-vision penetration is about 30% against nearly 100% in the US; and the move from monocular to binocular devices doubles the tubes needed per soldier.
  • Sovereign-content rules that hard-code Theon's eligibility: SAFE requires at least 65% of component cost to come from the EU, the European Economic Area or Ukraine; the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP) targets 50% European sourcing by 2030; and the Omnibus V package lengthens frameworks from seven to ten years. Meanwhile the US International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) keep US primes out of Europe above about 1,800 to 2,000 Figure of Merit.
  • Agency procurement: OCCAR-type buying is heading to about 40% of European procurement by 2030, and it funnels national tenders into single awards won by the largest qualified supplier.

Defence optronics grows at about twice the rate of defence spending, a compound annual growth rate of 12% to 13%. The drivers already show in Theon's orders: H1 2026 order intake rose 38.5% to 232.5 EURm, Q2 2026 was the strongest quarter outside a Q4 in the group's history, and the backlog has grown from 540 EURm at end-2023 to 1.46 EURbn.

Five headwinds exist, and they act on timing, price and the multiple rather than on demand. They are ranked below in order of bite.

Revenue through 2028 is paced by supply and delivery schedules, not by demand. The external picture splits cleanly into an A-grade tailwind on operations and a C-grade headwind on valuation and financing. The model therefore paces revenue by supply and schedules, which makes the FY2027 revenue cone narrow (-8% / +2%) for a company growing 24%. Tube availability is the one external force that could stop the backlog converting into revenue, and the same force caps revenue in the out-years.

Against the market: I agree that demand is not the debate, but most brokers have not put the tube cap into their out-year revenue. The sell-side narrative has moved to "execution, margin and cash" (Bernstein, 29 September 2026: the market "no longer pays more for a share because the company wins an order"). Deutsche Bank and Bernstein both know the tube cap as a fact, yet UBS forecasts 916 EURm and Deutsche Bank 923 EURm of FY2028 revenue against the model's 853 EURm.

Counter-case: the tube cap could lift, and a ceasefire could slow the options. Exosens' capacity ramp beat plan twice in 2026, its FY2026 guidance was raised on 17 September, and its capacity rises about 40% by end-2027. If Exosens' Q4 2026 release shows its Amplification volumes running ahead and Theon's allocation rises, FY2028 consensus revenue becomes reachable. A ceasefire would not remove the contracted backlog, but it would slow option exercise and, after 2027, re-open price competition for new frameworks; procurement cycles that compressed to 3 to 12 months during the war could revert to more than 30 months.

Score: 83, set by the Rater. European rearmament floored by policy to 2035, sovereign-content rules that hard-code Theon's eligibility, agency procurement funnelling awards to the largest qualified supplier and a 1.46 EURbn backlog make demand structural and visible (consensus sales growth p95 is honest, not a one-off); netted against the direct threats to those forces, the external tube cap that slows night-vision growth to 4-7% after FY2027 and agency buyer power on price. I place it a notch above the External change forces group's 76 because rates, credit spreads and sector de-rating act on the multiple, not on organic growth or margins, and just below Arteche, with Indra's cleaner budget-driven tailwind above.

#2 Internally-driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Conclusion: Theon's transformation is real, funded, already visible and led by an exceptional operator. Its cost lands below EBIT and on the multiple before its benefit lands on EPS, and its weak spots (capital discipline, governance scaffolding and disclosure of the lines that decide EPS) are exactly where the case's risk sits.

The founder is turning a night-vision assembler into a multi-domain European optronics group, and the shift already shows in the revenue mix. Night vision was 93% of FY2025 revenue. The November 2025 Capital Markets Day set three targets: 1 EURbn of revenue by 2029 (pulled forward a year), half of revenue outside night vision by 2029, and organic growth above 15% (the "supported by bolt-on M&A" qualifier has since been dropped). Revenue outside night vision was 24% of Q2 2026 revenue against 3% a year earlier, and at least 34% of H1 2026 order intake.

About 700 EURm has been committed in 18 months to resource the transformation, and guidance has been raised twice in FY2026, on margin as well as revenue.

The organisation is being built for integration rather than for further deals. The bench below the founder has been deliberately thickened: a deputy CEO, a CEO of Theon Sensors who leads post-merger integration, and Merio's founder retained as President and Chief Technology Officer. On 8 September 2026 management said that integration now takes priority over new acquisitions. A 30 USDm organic US investment programme (in Virginia and Oregon) has begun and is not in the model. The ARMED Next augmented-reality prototype is ahead of the Capital Markets Day timetable, and the fused ORION goggle has won its first NATO order.

The problems share one root, fast debt-funded expansion directed by the founder with thin governance, and they would compound together in a downturn. The eight weak spots are set out below.

The positive forces lift revenue and EBITDA faster than EPS until 2028, because their costs land below EBIT and on the multiple. Those costs are interest, amortisation of acquired intangibles, minority interests and management bandwidth. The organisational risk is four integrations in four countries at once, run from a homogeneous Greek head office by a CFO who has not yet consolidated a multinational group. The two small integrations (Kappa and Harder) have gone well; the large one (HGH, four times Kappa's size, French and software-heavy) has not started.

Against the market: the narrative has not yet discussed the related-party loans, the January 2027 board renewal or the treatment of amortisation in adjusted EBIT. The market already knows the leverage peak, the HGH price and the Exosens reversal. The January 2027 board renewal is a free governance option and a free risk at the same time. On amortisation, the H1 2026 bridge from reported to adjusted EBIT consists exactly of the non-recurring items, which suggests that acquired-intangible amortisation stays inside the company's adjusted EBIT; on that basis the FY2027 headline margin would show about 25.1% against the "above 26%" target with the business unchanged. I treat this as a communication risk that the company can avoid by redefining adjusted EBIT when HGH closes, as Exosens does.

Counter-case: the founder's recent choices point to a deleveraging phase. Since September he has put integration ahead of deals, dropped the Exosens board-seat plan when antitrust objections bit, and heard investors "demanding a lower leverage target" (per ING). A January board refresh that raises independence would be the first governance improvement since listing. Two events would make me downgrade the change forces from strong-but-costly to reckless: a further debt-funded acquisition before leverage is below 2.5x, or a third consecutive net-debt print worse than consensus.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. A large, funded and already-visible pivot from night-vision assembler to multi-domain optronics group (non-night-vision 3% to 24% of quarterly revenue, about 700 EURm of acquisitions, Kappa adding 11 points of H1 growth, guidance raised twice) is a large change force, but its cost lands below EBIT so the EPS benefit waits for 2028, and it is netted by weak capital-allocation discipline (the Exosens reversal, HGH at about 18x EBITDA), related-party loans, disclosure lapses and four integrations at once, with HGH not yet started; the covenant risk itself is left to topic 9. I sit above the group's 58 because the scale of the pivot and its early delivery weigh more than the group allowed, between Kitron and Redcare.

#3 Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Conclusion: Theon holds the number-one position in a benign, consolidating oligopoly. Lock-in, regulation and tube priority protect that position, not technology or price. The operating margin is an outlier, the cash line is weak, and the first-class founder-operator's soft spots are governance and capital discipline.

European man-portable night vision is a concentrated, benign, margin-first oligopoly, and market share has moved in only one direction: toward Theon. Theon holds 50% to 60% of the market; Safran and Thales hold 12% to 13% each, and both "avoid markets where Theon is strong"; the top three hold 75% to 85%. Qualification cycles of two to eight years and tube scarcity keep standard entrants out. Agency procurement consolidates awards toward the largest qualified supplier, and the 1 EURbn OCCAR award, the largest night-vision-goggle award in NATO history, is the proof. Theon grew revenue 40% to 60% a year from 2020 to 2024.

The industry structure has two pressure points, and both act on Theon's margin rather than its share. The first is buyer power through agency tenders: 100,000-unit awards carry volume discounts, and Theon's gross margin fell from 40.7% in FY2021 to 31.0% in FY2024 as contracts grew larger, before recovering to 35.1% in H1 2026 on mix. The second is a co-dependent upstream monopolist that is now also a downstream entrant: Theon is 40% of Exosens' revenue, and Exosens earns a gross margin of about 50% against Theon's 31% to 35%. Theon's route to market for OCCAR also runs through the Hensoldt-Theon joint venture, and Hensoldt is expanding its own optronics (its Optronics orders were 759 EURm in Q1 2026). In the segments Theon is entering (platforms, gimbals, and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance), it is a sub-scale entrant against Thales, Hensoldt, Safran, Elbit and NextVision, and has no moat yet.

Theon's moat rests on four protections, none of which is technology or price. The Greek cost advantage is deliberately shared with the customer, which is why market share drifts to Theon and why margins are stable rather than expanding. The business model is asset-light (capex about 4% to 5% of revenue) and labour-variable (headcount rose from 135 in 2020 to 1,044 by June 2026), so Theon's competitive position compounds mechanically while its financial outputs do not.

Theon's financial profile is outlier-high on the operating lines and weak on the lines that pay the shareholder. Theon's adjusted EBIT margin of 26.2% compares with about 13% at Hensoldt, 9% to 10% at Elbit and 27.3% at Exosens, which earns a 50% gross margin. ROCE was 31% in FY2024 and falls by construction to about 14% in FY2027, as about 560 EURm of goodwill, intangibles and the non-earning Exosens stake enter the capital base. Free cash flow was 58%, -63% and 17% of net income over FY2023 to FY2025, against 2.1x at Hensoldt and 0.6x at Exosens. Net working capital is 41% to 42% of revenue, against a 35% company target, MilDef's 31% and Renk's about 25%, and Theon shows no visible customer prepayments: advances were 1.5 EURm and contract liabilities 3.7 EURm at June 2026, whereas Hensoldt collects about 15% of order value in advance and Rheinmetall about 30%.

The founder is a first-class operator by his actions; the weak half of management is capital discipline, governance, communication and succession.

Proven strengths

  • A 40% revenue compound annual growth rate over six years at mid-20s margins
  • The IPO promises (Harder, Kappa) delivered within 18 months
  • The largest NATO night-vision-goggle award won
  • No salary for the founder, and 107 EURm of his own money in the rights issue
  • A cohesive team that has worked together for over 20 years
  • Outlier execution: the Paris Olympics deliveries; ARMED Next ahead of plan

Weak spots

  • Capital allocation: the Exosens reversal, HGH's price, the 30%-discount rights issue, the related-party loans
  • Governance: a controlled company with a 30% free float, and an exemption from the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission that makes creeping control costless
  • Communication: silence on the lines that decide EPS
  • Succession: the founder is 65 and has disclosed no plan

The culture is congruent in the Greek core (Great Place to Work Hellas three years running; 92% of staff rate management honest) and untested in the French and German engineering units.

Against the market: brokers describe the moat and the margin correctly but under-appreciate one negative and one positive. The negative is that the scarce technology and its profit pool sit upstream at Exosens, and Theon's attempts to own them (Harder, the Exosens stake) have so far bought a hedge, not a substitute. The positive is that agency consolidation is a structural market-share tailwind that will outlast the current cycle.

Counter-case: Harder's tubes and Exosens' choices could move the moat in either direction. If Harder's tubes gain NATO acceptance (they now reach a Figure of Merit above 2,000), Theon's dependence on Exosens eases materially. If Exosens prioritises its own devices or offers its 5G tubes to rivals, the moat narrows at its most important layer. The renewal of the Exosens supply agreement in 2030 is the structural event beyond the forecast horizon.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. Number one with 50-60% of a benign, consolidating European night-vision oligopoly, protected by an installed base, ITAR-free regulation and tube priority, but with no technology or pricing moat, dependence on an upstream monopolist that is turning competitor, a 38% customer, no moat in the new segments and weak governance; ROIC 20.3% (p91) and a 23% operating margin (p74) overstate the economics, since ROCE falls to about 14% as goodwill and the non-earning Exosens stake enter, new capital (HGH at about 18x EBITDA) earns far less, and FCF conversion is 17% (p28). Coherent with the four groups (76/68/56/64), close to Volex's design-in switching-cost business and above Linea Directa.

#4 Conservative guidance, sell-side expectations, and the delivery record

Conclusion: guidance is conservative and reliable on the lines it covers and silent on the lines that decide EPS. The record supports leaning revenue and EBIT above consensus and net debt worse than consensus, and the next move in consensus EPS is a mechanical accounting cut that is worth anticipating rather than fearing.

On the operating lines, Theon's record over 2.6 listed years is unbroken: under-promise, raise mid-year, over-deliver. FY2024 revenue (352.4 EURm) landed above the 330 to 350 EURm guidance range, and FY2025 revenue (443.4 EURm) landed above the first range of 410 to 430 EURm and within the raised range of 435 to 445 EURm; FY2025 EBIT beat consensus by 7%, and Q4 EBIT by 11%. For FY2026, Theon moved revenue guidance from 570 to 600 EURm to about 600 EURm and, at the H1 results, moved the margin target from "mid-twenties" to "above 26%", just when OCCAR dilution was the market's fear. H1 2026 beat Deutsche Bank's forecasts by 3.1% on revenue and 9.2% on EBIT (margin +150 basis points). The medium-term framework was upgraded in substance: 1 EURbn pulled forward a year, the bolt-on qualifier dropped, and the margin target raised to above 26%.

On the balance sheet, the record is equally unbroken in the other direction. Net debt printed 18% worse than consensus at Q1 2026 and 8.8% worse than Deutsche Bank's forecast at H1 2026.

Consensus sits on top of guidance for FY2026, and the company guides nothing below EBIT. For FY2026, revenue guidance (about 600 EURm) and consensus (600 EURm from six brokers, range 598 to 606 EURm) coincide; consensus EBIT of 155 EURm (25.8%) sits just below the above-26% floor, which suggests that some brokers deduct non-recurring items. For FY2027, consensus revenue of 743 EURm reflects the framework plus acquisitions (about 15% to 17% organic growth after 55 to 60 EURm of acquired sales) at a 26.8% margin, slightly above the model's 26.5%. The company gives no guidance on interest, tax, free cash flow, EPS or segment margins, and no covenant definition. Informal commentary runs ahead of formal guidance: options are "expected to be exercised shortly"; HGH will be "mid-single-digit EPS accretive" in 2027; pro-forma leverage would be "below 1.0x" if liquid assets were monetised; and ING says diversification is happening "much faster than the sell-side is modelling".

All seven brokers rate Theon Buy (mean target 39.88 EUR), but the consensus median hides two different models of the company. FY2027 consensus is revenue of 743 EURm, EBITDA of 203 to 208 EURm and EPS of 1.65 to 1.66 EUR. UBS has the highest FY2027 revenue (780 EURm) and the lowest EPS (1.42 EUR) because it carries interest and amortisation; Oddo has the reverse (712 EURm and 1.91 EUR). FY2026 EPS runs from 1.28 EUR (Deutsche Bank, after non-recurring items) to 1.95 EUR (Marex, including the Exosens fair-value marks), so the 1.50 EUR median mixes bases and the 10.7% FY2027 EPS growth it implies is an artefact. The FY2029 median of 2.05 EUR rests on three brokers and implies about 89m shares against 78.6m in issue.

Guidance is conservative where I can test it and silent where I disagree with consensus, which is favourable for the next two reporting events and neutral after them. The record supports leaning revenue and EBIT 1% to 3% above consensus for FY2026 and FY2027 (the model does, at 605 and 752 EURm) and leaning net debt worse than consensus. The one guided target the record says to lean against is the one the market is pricing: leverage below 2.5x in 2027.

A cut to FY2026 consensus EPS is coming that no broker has yet written down, and it is an accounting event, not an operating one. Exosens closed at 56.9 EUR on 30 October against 61.4 EUR at end-June, so the stake's H1 gain of 37.2 EURm reverses by about 23 EURm in H2, untaxed. The brokers who include the fair-value marks (ING at 1.79 EUR and Marex at 1.95 EUR) must each take about 0.30 EUR off FY2026 EPS when they update, and the FactSet mean will fall from 1.56 EUR to about 1.47 EUR with no operating change. The dashboard's sell-side momentum letter (C) will read that fall as deterioration; an informed investor can see through it.

Against the market: I agree with consensus on FY2027 EBIT and am below it on every line beneath interest and tax. The model's FY2027 EBIT (199 EURm) is at the consensus median. The model's FY2027 adjusted EPS after minorities is 2% below consensus (1.63 EUR against 1.66 EUR); its net income is 5% to 8% below for FY2027 to FY2029 because of interest and tax; and its free cash flow is 19% to 26% below through FY2028.

Counter-case: the beats should continue, but at a smaller amplitude. The past beats came from a demand-pull, short-cycle, net-cash phase; the coming phase is fixed-price, supply-capped, leveraged and multi-country. If the FY2026 results on 19 March 2027 show an underlying tax rate near 30% rather than 25%, or year-end working capital above 42% of revenue, the lean against the balance sheet should get stronger still.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. An unbroken under-promise, raise and beat record on revenue and EBIT over all 2.6 listed years (FY2024 and FY2025 delivered above range, FY2026 raised twice on revenue and margin, H1 2026 EBIT 9% above Deutsche Bank) with conservative operating guidance today, against a short record, silence below EBIT and net debt printing worse than consensus at both 2026 prints, which is the leverage target the market prices; the -2% three-month EPS revision (p28) is an accounting mark, not a miss. Between the Guidance (72) and Sell-side (48) groups weighted to guidance, just above Kerry and below Ithaca's fuller record.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out, feedback loops

Conclusion: revenue growth converts to EBIT growth about one-for-one, and to EPS growth below that until 2027 and above it from 2028. The business has no profit-amplifying mechanism inside the P&L; its only amplifier is financial leverage, which taxes the next 18 months and pays back after.

Theon has real pricing power but does not use it, and will not use it before the OCCAR contract ends in 2029. Theon sets prices from its costs rather than from what the market will bear. Device prices rose 2.5x to 3.0x after 2022 while Theon's gross margin fell from 40.7% to 31.0% over FY2021 to FY2024, because the price rise was tube cost and scarcity rent captured upstream by Exosens. OCCAR, about 35% to 40% of FY2027 to FY2029 revenue, carries fixed prices with annual adjustments capped near 10%. OCCAR's tube cost appears fixed for the ordered volumes through Exosens' own 500 EURm OCCAR order at about 2,500 EUR a tube (below Bernstein's 2026 average of 2,703 EUR), so the feared tube-cost squeeze on OCCAR is partly hedged; the exposed element is the non-tube 45% of OCCAR's cost, mainly German and Greek wages. Bilateral and export contracts pass Exosens' 3% to 4% annual price rises through at a constant gross-margin percentage. Blended, price adds about 1.5 points a year to night-vision revenue growth and nothing to margin. The unused pricing power comes from scarcity, lock-in, a 15% to 20% discount to peers that could be narrowed, and a "much thinner" discount on fused goggles.

Operating leverage is low, rising slowly and asymmetric. Tubes are 60% to 65% of night-vision cost and assembly labour flexes with volume, so the fixed block (SG&A, expensed R&D and fixed overhead) is only about 9% to 11% of revenue. The fixed block is stepping up: headcount rose 55% in a year, and the Athens plant (from Q2 2027), Zaventem and the acquired engineering teams all add fixed cost. A 10% revenue shortfall cuts EBIT by 11% to 13%; a 5% revenue beat earns an incremental margin of 32% to 35%, which lifts EBIT by about 6%. Within the year, Q4 carries 30% to 35% of sales and most of the fixed-cost absorption, so a 10% slip in Q4 revenue moves the full-year margin by 0.5 to 0.7 points. In this value chain the scarce-component maker owns the operating leverage (60% of Exosens' cost is fixed); the assembler does not.

Cost-out adds about nothing to the margin, but the cash levers are real. Identifiable efficiencies (group purchasing, Harder tubes on non-NATO lines and shared R&D) total about 5 to 8 EURm a year by FY2029, and wage localisation and new plants consume them. Theon has no cost programme and no quantified cost synergy; its only synergy target is 30 EURm of revenue by 2029. The cost programmes that worked elsewhere (L3Harris' LHX NeXt, Thales' COVID plan and Hensoldt-ESG) removed large duplicated overheads, which a lean founder-run company does not have. The cash levers are the working-capital ratio (each point is worth 7.5 EURm at FY2027 revenue and 10 EURm at FY2030 revenue) and the end of integration costs (non-recurring items of 8.5, 4 and 2 EURm, then nil).

Financial leverage is the only amplifier, and it cuts both ways. At the mid-2027 leverage peak, a 10% EBITDA miss becomes about a 15% EPS miss, adds about 0.3x of leverage and delays the sub-2.5x print by about a year. An extra 100 basis points on Euribor costs about 6 EURm, or 0.06 EUR of EPS (-3.5%); interest-rate swaps are in place, but their coverage is undisclosed. Interest cover is comfortable at 8x to 10x. From FY2028 the amplifier reverses, and falling debt adds 1 to 2 points a year to EPS growth.

The feedback loops switch regime in 2028, from a balancing loop that caps EPS to a reinforcing loop that lifts it. To end-2027 the balancing loop dominates the shareholder's lines: growth absorbs working capital, which raises net debt and interest, which caps EPS and acquisitions. A second negative loop runs from de-rating to debt-funding to more leverage and to further de-rating. The reinforcing revenue loops are real (the installed base leads to the next frameworks and to clip-on upgrades; largest-buyer status earns tube priority, which wins the largest awards), but they hit the tube cap, so they lengthen the backlog rather than lift annual revenue. From FY2028 the growth-and-working-capital loop flips: slower growth absorbs less cash, net debt and interest fall, EPS grows faster than EBIT and, if the multiple follows, the cost of capital falls.

Behind both regimes, a slow balancing loop acts on volume. Exosens, which depends on Theon for 40% of its revenue, is diversifying (NVLS, BiNOD and Sturbridge), which caps the growth of Theon's tube allocation after OCCAR and raises the stakes of the 2030 supply renewal. Two developments could change the timing: a stake sale would break the negative loop and start the positive one about a year early, and customer prepayments on new frameworks (Hensoldt's mechanism) would neutralise the balancing loop at once, although there is no evidence that Theon receives them.

Against the market: no broker frames FY2028's deleveraging as arithmetic rather than execution, and that is the positive this memo adds. The sell-side models a flat margin and knows the interest drag. On my arithmetic, OCCAR pricing and wage localisation fully offset the "mix shift to tube-free products lifts margins" narrative that management promotes.

Counter-case: faster scaling outside night vision, or indexation and prepayments in new frameworks, would change these conclusions. Hensoldt's Optronics EBITDA margin rose from 1.3% to 12.2% in a year on real fixed-cost leverage. If Theon's lines outside night vision scale faster than the fixed block built for them, their incremental margin above 30% would show as a rising group margin from FY2028. Evidence of price indexation or prepayments in new frameworks would change the pricing and cash conclusions together.

Score: 30, set by the Rater. The structure has little gearing: tubes are 60-65% of night-vision cost and assembly labour flexes with volume, so the fixed block is only 9-11% of revenue and a 10% revenue move is an 11-13% EBIT move; pricing power is latent and deliberately unused under fixed-price OCCAR to 2029, there is no cost-out scope, and the only amplifier is financial leverage, which taxes EPS to 2027 before reversing. Forecast EPS grows about 17% a year against revenue about 21% (a ratio near 0.8 against the Universe's typical 2), so it sits near the 25 level, lifted slightly by the arithmetic deleveraging from FY2028.

#6 Forecast financials

Conclusion: revenue more than doubles by FY2030 at a flat 26.4% margin, EPS compounds at about 18% a year to FY2028 and 11% after, and free cash flow turns steadily positive for the first time. Growth and margins will not exceed the past, but the quality of the compounding will.

Five businesses build the revenue line: night vision slows as the tube cap binds, and the rest of the group supplies the growth.

Night vision assumes tube volume plus 1.5% price a year, with OCCAR at about 300 to 330 EURm a year in 2027 to 2029. Organic growth outside night vision comes from thermal clip-ons (such as IRIS-C for OCCAR's IRCOD programme, with a 50 EURm order plus 150 EURm of options), the Kappa and PHYLAX platforms, Harder's third-party sales, ORION and ARMED. Group revenue reaches 1 EURbn in FY2030, a year after the company's ambition. Capex runs at 31 to 45 EURm a year; acquisitions are 377 EURm in FY2026 and 295 EURm in FY2027 (HGH), then bolt-ons only; the model assumes no disposal.

Growth and margins will not beat the past, but EBIT now keeps pace with revenue and cash finally rises steadily. Revenue growth is double-digit in every year to FY2029 and compounds at 24% a year to FY2028 and 18% to FY2030, half the 52% of FY2020 to FY2025. The slowdown is built in: the tube cap binds, the revenue base is three times its FY2023 size, and the order cycle peaked in FY2025 at a 3.0x book-to-bill. The margin does not rise, but it stops falling after losing eight points in four years, so EBIT growth now equals revenue growth where it historically lagged; that is the one respect in which the next four years beat the last four. EPS growth of about 18% a year to FY2028 compares with about 42% a year over FY2023 to FY2025, and comes with the opposite mix: a flat share count and heavy interest, instead of negligible interest and 26% more shares.

The most important change is in cash. Free cash flow moves from erratic (21, -42 and 14 EURm over FY2023 to FY2025) to steadily rising, and FY2028 is the first year that will test the improvement.

Against consensus: the model is at consensus on the operating lines for FY2026 and FY2027, and below it on out-year revenue, net income and free cash flow. Each gap has a specific cause.

Counter-case: the upside to the forecasts sits in three places, and so does the downside. The upside: Exosens raising Theon's tube allocation (the FY2028 revenue line); MilDef-style working capital (MilDef took its ratio from 41% to 31% in a year while growing 72%; Theon reaching its 35% target by FY2029 would release a further 38 EURm and take leverage to about 1.4x); and a stake sale (lower interest). The downside: OCCAR phasing; OCCAR's gross margin in its first bulk year, for which the record has no precedent; and a tax rate that prints nearer 30%. I would raise the FY2028 revenue line on an allocation announcement and cut the margin line on an H2 2026 gross margin below 34%.

Score: 91, set by the Rater. Squarely in the A band (15 to 30%) on contracted, double-digit revenue growth every year; placed low in the band because the margin is flat at about 26.4% rather than rising, part of the growth is bought and debt-funded (HGH, Merio, the Safran joint venture), and growth decelerates to 14% then 9% as the tube cap binds.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, consensus and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion: upgrades to revenue and EBIT guidance and consensus are more likely than not inside 12 months; EPS consensus is more likely to drift down for accounting and interest reasons; and the narrative turns only on a balance-sheet print or a stake sale. The upgrade skew is therefore positive on the operating lines and neutral on the line the market is pricing.

Theon's mechanism for raising guidance is intact for FY2027. First guidance for a year is set from scheduled backlog with the options excluded, and the mid-year raise is the options coming in. I expect first FY2027 guidance of about 750 to 760 EURm on 19 March 2027. At the same FY2026 results, I put an 85% probability on FY2026 revenue at or above 600 EURm and 80% on a margin at or above 26% on the company's basis. At the H1 2027 results, a cut would need an OCCAR tranche or a Bundestag approval to slip a quarter, or a ceasefire to pause option exercise. Over 18 months, the probability that operating guidance is raised at least once is about 60%, and that it is cut at least once about 20%; both can happen.

The margin target faces an optical problem, and the medium-term ambitions are the targets most likely to slip. There is a 25% probability of a wording change that reads as a margin reduction with the business unchanged, unless the company excludes purchase-price amortisation from adjusted EBIT when HGH closes. The medium-term ambitions (1 EURbn of revenue by 2029, half of revenue outside night vision, and organic growth above 15% from FY2028) are most likely to be pushed out at the FY2028 guidance in March 2028.

Consensus is likely to repeat the last twelve months' pattern: operating lines up, EPS down, targets flat. Over the next twelve months I expect operating estimates held or nudged up 1% to 3% at the FY2026 results and at the H1 2027 raise. I expect EPS estimates cut in small steps for three reasons: accounting (the Exosens mark reversal, within one to three months); interest and tax (at the annual report, 2% to 5% for the brokers who have not modelled them); and HGH consolidation moving from January to April (a small negative headline revision with no information in it). I also expect FY2028 and FY2029 revenue estimates cut 2% to 5% as the tube cap enters the guided year. The breadth of EPS revisions will read negative in most months, and will turn positive only on a stake sale (FY2028 EPS +4% to +5%) or on a June 2027 leverage print at or below 2.9x with working capital at or below 40%. A first Hold rating in all-Buy coverage becomes likely if net debt prints worse than consensus a third time.

The narrative has already moved from "the largest NATO night-vision award" to "can a levered, founder-led acquirer convert backlog into cash", and the share price sits on that question. Four events would move the narrative: end-2026 net debt near 250 EURm (the first print not worse than expected); the HGH purchase-price allocation and the adjusted-EBIT definition in March 2027; June 2027 leverage, reported in September 2027; and a stake sale at any time. The narrative has missed two positives and five individually small negatives, which would surface at the annual report.

The case does not need upgrades to work; it needs the balance-sheet question to close. The upgrade skew is positive on EBIT and revenue (the lines the market says it will not pay for), negative on EPS for about six months (for reasons an informed investor can discount) and binary on the narrative. The model's FY2027 adjusted EPS (1.66 EUR) is already at consensus.

Against the market: the sell-side treats "below 2.5x in 2027" as a management promise; I treat it as a coin toss without a stake sale and a certainty with one. Consensus is more optimistic than I am on free cash flow and the out-years, and less convinced than I am that FY2028's deleveraging is mechanical.

Counter-case: one event would lift out-year consensus, and one would turn every revision negative. Exosens raising Theon's tube allocation would lift out-year revenue consensus rather than cut it. A Q4 2026 collection slip that prints net debt 10% worse than consensus would turn the whole revision picture negative, including EBITDA, because the market would start pricing an equity raise.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Operating guidance is more likely raised than cut (about 60% at least one raise in 18 months, first FY2027 guide likely at or above consensus), but a 1-3% raise on 24% revenue growth is small on Richard's scale, while EPS consensus, the line that drives the price, is more likely to fall (the Exosens mark reversal of about 6% on FY2026, interest and tax, the tube cap cutting FY2028 revenue 2-5%) and the narrative turns only on a binary balance-sheet print or stake sale. Coherent with the fourth-set group's 44, between Kerry's modest upside and Carlsberg's mixed picture.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and peers

Conclusion: Theon's operating momentum is among the strongest in its peer group, yet its sell-side EPS momentum is flat to negative and its technical momentum is the worst in the group. About three-quarters of that divergence comes from Theon's own leverage story, and only Theon's own prints will close it.

Guidance momentum is positive. Guidance was raised twice in FY2026 (revenue to about 600 EURm, margin to above 26%), the medium-term framework was upgraded, and informal commentary runs ahead of formal guidance.

Sell-side momentum scores C on the dashboard (28 October) because FY2027 estimates have split: EBITDA and sales estimates rose over every period while EPS estimates edged down. The target price rose 2% over one month and 1% over three; the share of Buy ratings rose 11 points over three months to 100%; and the dashboard's revision-momentum score is 6. The split is the leverage transmission, not a demand problem: Theon's operating estimates are the strongest in the peer group except MilDef's, while its EPS estimates are flat to down.

Narrative momentum is negative to neutral. ING cut its target to 38 EUR from 42.50 EUR on 15 September on sector multiples alone; Deutsche Bank called the Exosens reversal "capital allocation volatility" and cut EPS 5% for interest; nobody has downgraded the shares. Deutsche Bank's 2 November preview is titled "No surprises expected".

Technical momentum scores F on the dashboard (30 October), and the shares have stopped trending with their sector. The price of 30.42 EUR sits at its 50-day average (30.44 EUR) and below its 150-day (31.94 EUR) and 200-day (31.54 EUR) averages, 3.6% below the latter, although the 200-day average has risen in eleven of the last twelve months. Relative strength is at the 32nd percentile of the universe; the 52-week range is 23.34 to 39.50 EUR; and about 115,000 shares (about 7.8 USDm) trade a day. The rolling six-month R-squared to the peer basket is 24% (beta 0.80), down from 30% to 34% in the order-driven phase of late 2025.

MilDef, the peer with the closest operating shape, shows what Theon's chart can look like once the balance-sheet question closes. MilDef is a framework assembler whose leverage peaked at 2.6x to 2.9x in 2025 and fell to 1.0x within six quarters as its working-capital ratio fell ten points; it is now the group's best-rated stock on all three dashboard letters. Theon has the weakest technical letter and the lowest P/E in the group.

Operating momentum and share-price momentum have decoupled, and the decoupling is Theon's own. A multiple that is three-quarters company-driven will respond to Theon's prints without needing the sector, which suits a case whose catalysts are balance-sheet events. The flip side is that nothing outside the company will rescue the shares in the meantime, and a sector sell-off still reaches them (beta 0.8 to a basket that fell 30% in May to June 2026).

Against the market: I accept the dashboard's F and C letters as facts, but I read the price pattern as one that precedes a turn, not a collapse. The last three months combine an idiosyncratic fall, rising estimates, unanimous coverage and a dated catalyst. The technical letter will be the last of the three letters to move.

Counter-case: two technical signals would settle the reading. A break below the 52-week low of 23.34 EUR on company news (a collection slip, a covenant headline or a share placement by the shareholder Venetus) would convert the drift into a downtrend. A close above the 200-day average, held for a month after the 9 November update, would be the first technical sign of the turn.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. Mixed measures give C; within it the number sits low because consensus EPS is down 2% over three months (p28), technicals are the worst in the peer group (below the 150 and 200-day averages, -12.6% over three months) and the narrative is negative to neutral, offset by two guidance raises, EBITDA estimates up 16% in a year and 100% Buy ratings, which are not strong enough to lift the letter.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations

Conclusion: the case is simple to state and to monitor, with five correlated drivers explaining most of the variance. It is narrow on revenue, wide and skewed down on FY2027 EPS, bimodal on leverage, and exposed to sudden sector sentiment shocks that a geared small-cap absorbs first. Riskiness is therefore medium-high in the 18-month window, and it falls sharply once leverage is below 2.5x.

The case is simple: a contracted revenue path paced by tubes and call-offs, a flat margin, and a leverage curve that peaks in mid-2027 and falls by arithmetic from 2028. Three drivers explain most of FY2027's variance: OCCAR and German call-off timing against a fixed tube supply, the working-capital ratio, and HGH's contribution against its debt cost. A fourth driver, Exosens' share price, moves reported earnings but nothing real. A short monitoring list covers all four:

  • Bundestag approvals and Hensoldt's order intake, as proxies for German call-offs
  • Exosens' quarterly Amplification volumes
  • Theon's quarterly working-capital ratio and joint-venture receivables (22.7 EURm at June 2026 against 6.6 EURm at end-2025, rising into the OCCAR ramp)
  • The HGH closing date and purchase-price allocation

Concentration makes the case dangerous as well as simple. Theon has no second large customer, no second NATO-grade tube supplier and no second deleveraging lever beyond the stake, so the forecast cannot be de-risked from inside the company.

Five judgements move the shares; the table works through each one from the FY2027 base case. The base case is revenue of 752 EURm, adjusted EBIT of 199.2 EURm, net financial items of -27 EURm, pre-tax profit of 172.2 EURm, tax at 25%, net income of 129.2 EURm on 77.6m shares and EPS of 1.66 EUR, with EBITDA of about 210 EURm and end-2027 net debt of about 522 EURm (2.48x).

The 18-month cone is predictable where the case is least valuable and event-driven where it is priced.

One shock, a ceasefire or a Bundestag delay, would move three of the five judgements at once, all through leverage. The shock would slow call-offs (A), leave the inventory bought for them on the balance sheet (B) and raise net debt in the half-year in which HGH's cash goes out, while the accompanying sector sell-off would mark the stake down (C) at the moment it is needed. The May to June 2026 episode showed the sector leg (peers -30%, Theon -4.8%) without the operating leg, because deliveries were not yet weighted to OCCAR; from Q1 2027 both legs move together.

The fundamental shocks are low-probability, hedged and trackable; the perception shocks are sudden and unhedged. Theon is exposed to perception shocks because it has a 30% free float, trades 7.8 USDm a day and sits in a market that penalises fragility. The perception shocks include ceasefire headlines, US policy moves, a Rheinmetall or Hensoldt stumble (Rheinmetall reports on 5 November; Boxer options are due in December), a placement by Venetus, an Exosens de-rating, and a covenant headline when the HGH cash goes out. Disclosure helps on operations (quarterly revenue by product category, orders, backlog, options, gross margin, working-capital ratio and leverage) but not on the financial lines: between annual reports there is no interest, tax, cash-flow statement, covenant definition or OCCAR phasing.

The downside in the shares is set by the multiple, not by the fundamental shocks. A fall to a fair trough multiple of 11x to 12x would take the shares down about 21% to 28%, to about 22 to 24 EUR, near the 52-week low. The stress case (the 10th-percentile multiple of 9.86x on a 10% EPS cut) is a fall of about 34% to 41%, to 18 to 20 EUR, which matches Deutsche Bank's free-cash-flow-yield valuation of 18 EUR and the 17.40 EUR rights-issue price.

Sector precedents say that a large fall with a full order book usually reflects the company's own cash, debt or share issuance, and reverses when the cash arrives; Theon is in that pattern. After an order boom, defence shares are paid for delivery, margin and cash, not for orders. Leverage and dilution after acquisitions are the sector's recurrent failure mode: Exail's iXblue deal, funded with payment-in-kind debt, ended in a sale and a refinancing from 12% to 4%, and Theon's own December 2025 rights issue fits the pattern. Fixed-price contracts in a period of inflation hurt L3Harris until an activist arrived. Programme cancellation can be sudden and uninsurable (Hensoldt's 12.8 EURbn F126 frigate programme, June 2026). Small, geared names are sold first in risk-off markets. The cycle itself is paced by supply and policy to 2029; the cyclical risk sits in 2029 to 2030, when OCCAR re-tenders and a ceasefire could bring "aggressive price wars" into excess capacity, and the model allows only about 0.3 points of margin for that risk.

Against the market: the market prices the leverage worry as a single risk; I see leverage as the common factor behind four correlated risks, which fattens the tail. I also see the stake as converting most of that tail from dilution into de-risking, which the market has not priced either.

What would change my view. Confirmation that the September 2026 financing package reset the covenant to 3.5x with pro-forma EBITDA, or an announced hedge of the stake, would lower the riskiness a notch. A third worse-than-consensus net-debt print or a new debt-funded deal would raise it.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. Revenue is contracted and narrow and the drivers are few and tracked quarterly, but FY2027 EPS is skewed down (-17%/+9%), leverage peaks at 2.9x against a covenant of 3.5x or possibly 3.0x (a 2-16% cushion), the risks are correlated through leverage (a ceasefire or Bundestag slip hits call-offs, working capital and the stake together), there is one large customer and one NATO-grade tube supplier, a dilution precedent, and a 30%-float small-cap that sector shocks reach first. Between the two Risks groups (40 and 54) towards the lower, below OMV Petrom and a little above D'Ieteren's more complex and higher-levered holding.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: Theon is Bottoming. The operating thesis is broadening while the share has de-rated on its own balance sheet, and the turn up is dated to the net-debt prints of March and September 2027 unless a stake sale brings it forward.

The dashboard's Phases rule places Theon at Bottoming (2 November 2026), and the three ingredients line up. Current momentum is poor on the share (technical F, relative strength at the 32nd percentile, an idiosyncratic three-month fall of 12.6%) and strong on the business (guidance raised twice, order intake +38.5%, EBITDA estimates +16% in a year). The scope for upgrades is positive on EBIT and dated on the narrative. The risk factors are concentrated in one dated test. The multiple has fallen from a two-year median of 17.0x to about 15x while estimates rose, and the price has made a sequence of lower highs since May (33.1 EUR) while holding a higher low than the 2024 trough.

The business and the share are in two different phases at once. On the operating thesis, Theon is in the "thesis broadening" phase: the night-vision franchise is proven, the platform, intelligence-and-surveillance, gimbal and tube legs are being added, and each quarter's mix print has confirmed the direction. On the share, Theon is Bottoming, because the market has re-priced it from an order story to a cash story and is waiting for the first cash print. The two phases coexist because the operating staircase of events is dense, while the financial staircase has one decisive step, the H1 2027 leverage print in September 2027, with end-2026 net debt on 19 March 2027 as the early read. A stake sale would collapse the two phases into one and start the turn immediately.

Against the market: the honest reading is Bottoming with a dated turn, between the sell-side's "turning up" and the price's "stalling". The sell-side's unanimous Buy with 40 EUR targets implies "turning up" already, and the price implies "stalling". The stock will not re-rate on the operating prints between now and March 2027, however good, and it will re-rate on the balance-sheet prints, in whichever direction they go.

Every trigger that would move the share to the next phase, or back, is a balance-sheet event.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The computed Bottoming is right for the share (relative strength p32, a 12.6% idiosyncratic fall, EPS revisions slightly negative, multiple down from 17x to 15x) while the operating thesis is broadening (EBITDA estimates +16%, guidance raised twice, mix confirming); the turn is dated to net-debt prints in March and September 2027 unless the stake is sold, so this is Bottoming with a visible but not imminent turn. Better than Greggs' early Turning on falling volumes, below Banca Generali's late Reinforcing.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion: the Phases guideline of 13.92x understates a bottoming stock whose estimates are rising and whose history is only 31 months long. My probability-weighted fair multiple is about 14.5x to 15x today, for which the model's 14.8x is a fair proxy; it rises to the 15.7x to 17x median range once leverage is below 2.5x and falls toward 11.8x if leverage stays above.

The Phases page sets the guideline fair multiple for a Bottoming stock at 13.92x, 5% below today's 14.71x. The guideline is the 30th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history of two-year-forward P/E. The model was run at 14.80x, between the Selector's 14.4x "conservative" and 15.7x "prudent" bands, and that multiple drives the return in topic #12. The stock's own range (the dashboard's ten-year percentiles, outliers excluded) is 11.8x at the 10th percentile, 15.7x at the median, 18.2x at the 75th and 20.9x at the 90th. FactSet's five-year weekly series gives a 25th-to-75th-percentile range of 11.16x to 17.79x, with today at the 42nd percentile, and a two-year median of 17.01x, with today at the 24th.

I set the fair multiple today at about 14.5x to 15x, so the model's 14.8x is the right proxy and the Phases page's 13.92x is a little low, for three reasons.

  1. The history is short and its low end is unrepresentative. The "ten-year" history is only 31 months long (the IPO was in February 2024), and its lower third is the 2024 trough, when an unknown Greek small-cap traded at 7.6x to 10.7x before the sector re-rated. A 30th percentile drawn from that series understates the floor for a company that has since tripled its revenue and won the largest night-vision-goggle award in NATO history.
  2. Theon's uncertainty sits on the balance sheet, not in the earnings. The Bottoming discount is meant to pay for forecast uncertainty, but FY2027 EBIT is at consensus and the FY2027 revenue cone runs only from -8% to +2%.
  3. The multiple should be anchored to Theon's own history and weighted by the two balance-sheet branches. The multiple is three-quarters company-driven, so peers at 20x to 28x are the wrong anchor. Weighting the branch in which the leverage question closes well (about 65%) and the branch in which it does not (about 35%) gives 14.7x.

For the decision, the fair multiple has two stages, and the leverage test divides them. While the leverage question is open, the fair multiple is where the stock trades, 14x to 15x: a stock in peak operating delivery will not be paid a peak-delivery multiple until its balance sheet clears. Once leverage is below 2.5x or the stake is sold, the stock's own median (15.7x) and two-year median (17x) become reachable on earnings that consensus already carries; that is the 15% to 20% re-rating sized in the earlier analysis. If the June 2027 print fails, the fair multiple is the trough band of 11x to 12x for as long as the fix is in doubt. Sector exit multiples are normalising toward about 13x EV/EBIT, and Theon already trades near 13x to 14x FY2027 EV/EBIT after adding HGH's cash cost and deducting the stake, so further sector compression has less room to hurt Theon than peers on 20x to 28x P/E.

Against the market: I agree with brokers that cash conversion causes the discount, but I think the discount is dated rather than structural. Deutsche Bank's EV/EBIT target multiple of 12.6x to 13.5x, set at a 15% discount to Exosens, and Bernstein's framing that investors are "penalising leverage" both attribute the discount to cash conversion.

What would change my view. A tightened or breached covenant would make the trough band the fair multiple. Evidence of customer prepayments, or a working-capital ratio below 38%, would justify moving toward the median before the leverage print.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. Neutral on both measures gives C; the number sits in the middle of the band because both readings lean slightly cheap, but the cheapness is partly deserved for a Bottoming stock with an open leverage question and a 31-month history whose low third is the 2024 trough, and the 0.66x cohort discount is its normal one.

#12 Total shareholder return

Conclusion: at 14.8x the model returns +12.8% to end-2027 and +29.2% to mid-2029, almost entirely from earnings, against a 9.6% de-rating drag. The multiple leg is the swing factor, worth about 40 points of 18-month return across the plausible range; the earnings leg is the dependable part.

The return of record is the model's, at the 14.80x guideline multiple, from 29.20 EUR on 28 October 2026.

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedValue per shareDividendsMultipleEarnings
To 31 December 2027 (the 18-month column)+12.8%+10.9%32.93 EUR+2.4%-9.6%+22.2%
To 30 June 2029 (the three-year column)+29.2%+10.1%37.73 EUR+3.9%-9.6%+38.6%

The de-rating leg is large because the model starts from a higher multiple than FactSet. The model's two-year-forward P/E today is 16.4x on its own EPS, which is below consensus EPS, so the model's starting multiple is higher than FactSet's 15.1x and its de-rating leg is correspondingly larger.

Earnings drive the return, the multiple is the swing factor, and dividends are small. The earnings leg is dependable: two-year-forward EPS rises about 22% by end-2027 and 39% by mid-2029 as FY2028 and FY2029 EPS (1.91 and 2.18 EUR) replace FY2026 and FY2027 EPS (1.36 and 1.66 EUR) in the forward blend. Those earnings rest on revenue that is contracted through FY2027 and tube-paced after, at a flat margin, with interest peaking in FY2027 and falling after. The multiple leg is a 9.6% drag because the model's starting multiple (16.4x) is above the guideline; the balance sheet, not the sector, sets this leg. The dividend leg is small (a 20% to 30% payout, 0.32 to 0.53 EUR a share over FY2026 to FY2029, a yield of about 1.1% to 1.7%) and stays small until leverage is below 2x; there is no buyback beyond the incentive plan.

The 18-month return ranges from about -10% to about +38% across the plausible exit multiples (earnings leg +22.2%, dividends +2.4%).

When the earnings leg moves with the multiple, the 18-month return ranges from about -23% to about +39%. The bear FY2027 (EPS 1.38 EUR), carried into FY2028 (about 1.62 EUR), cuts the earnings leg from +22% to about +4%: at 14.8x the 18-month return is about -4%, and at the 11.8x multiple that would accompany the bear case, about -23%. The bull case (FY2027 EPS about 1.78 EUR with a stake sale, FY2028 about 2.00 EUR) lifts the earnings leg to about +32%: at 17x the 18-month return is about +39%.

The shape of the outcome: because the multiple is bimodal with the balance sheet, so is the return. On the 65% branch (the target met narrowly, or the stake sold), the 18-month return is in the +19% to +29% range; on the 35% branch it is in the -10% to +6% range, and in the tail with a discounted equity raise it is about -20% to -25%. The probability-weighted 18-month return is close to the model's +13%, with a right tail fatter than the arithmetic suggests, because a stake sale would also raise FY2028 EPS by 5% and remove the reported-EPS noise. Over three years the earnings leg does most of the work on every branch, and even the trough multiple gives a small positive return: two-year-forward EPS at mid-2029 (about 2.45 EUR, the FY2030 and FY2031 blend) at 11.8x is about 29 EUR, plus about 1.1 EUR of dividends, against 29.20 EUR today.

Against the market: the sell-side's 30% upside is my bull branch, not my base case. The mean target of 39.88 EUR implies about 20x to 21x FY2028 consensus EPS: a peer-style multiple on earnings the brokers themselves are cutting. I think the earnings are right, and that the multiple needs the balance-sheet event first.

What would change my view. A stake sale would move me to the bull branch at once; a Q4 2026 collection slip would move me to the bear branch's multiple before its earnings.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. In the C band (10 to 20%), about 57 on the scale at 12.8%; moved down for today's higher price and the bimodal shape with a fat lower tail (-10% to +6% on the 35% branch, -20% to -25% with a discounted raise), only partly offset by the stake-sale right tail; the three-year +29% (about 10% a year) confirms a market-like return.

#13 Summary conclusion

Theon is the best-positioned European night-vision franchise at the moment the market has stopped paying for night-vision franchises.

Theon's operating case is unusually predictable. Demand is contracted and floored by policy; revenue is paced by a tube supply the company has locked in to 2030; the margin is held flat by offsetting mix effects whose components are visible each quarter; and guidance has been beaten and raised at every test since listing.

Theon's financial case is unusually binary. A debt-funded transformation takes leverage to a 2.9x peak in mid-2027 and to 2.48x at end-2027 against a 2.5x promise, under a covenant whose level the company has not confirmed. A liquid, tax-free, non-yielding 283 EURm stake in Theon's supplier could settle the whole question on any day management chooses.

The market has priced the worry. The stock trades at the 39th to 42nd percentile of its own multiple and at a 25% to 50% discount to electronics peers, with estimates rising, coverage unanimous and the catalyst dated.

For an investor who can hold through 10 to 11 months of good operating prints that will not re-rate the stock, the fundamental skew is modestly positive. The probability of upgrades is positive on EBIT, negative on EPS for accounting reasons that are visible in advance, and binary on the narrative. The three-year return is earnings-led and positive on almost every branch, and the 18-month return is a bet on a balance sheet that management can win by decision rather than by execution. The wider the covenant cushion proves and the earlier the stake is sold, the more Theon is a straightforward compounding story at a trough multiple; the narrower the cushion and the later the sale, the more Theon is a geared small-cap in a market that penalises fragility.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 77, set by the Rater. Strong structural tailwinds (83) and a large, delivering transformation (66) drive A-grade EPS growth of about 17% a year (91), so the expected change is material and clearly positive, but the business model converts it without amplification (30) and the cost of the transformation lands below EBIT until 2028, which keeps it at the bottom of the B band, in line with the memo's B.

Foundations' Robustness: 62, set by the Rater. A number-one position with lock-in, regulation and tube priority (quality 66) and a clean operating delivery record (76) are robust, but one upstream supplier that is also a competitor, a 38% customer, 17% cash conversion, leverage near an unconfirmed covenant and weak governance leave the foundations above typical yet short of the top quartile, consistent with the memo's C.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 70, set by the Rater. The case fits 'CfC clearing in a high-quality business on a Q2 multiple, reversion to normal' cleanly, with one identifiable concern, a dated test, a liquid lever to clear it and estimates rising while the multiple fell; the fit is less crisp because the clearing is a coin toss without the stake, the business is not low-cyclicality and an EPS-upgrade overlay blurs the edges.

Case Riskiness: 42, set by the Rater. Following topic 9 (42): the operating forecasts are simple and trackable, but the EPS cone is skewed down, the leverage outcome is bimodal near a covenant of unconfirmed level and the drivers are correlated through leverage in a small-float stock exposed to sector shocks, so risk is medium-high over the 18-month window.
